note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

precepts.why:
The Most High is “Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children”.

David confessed, “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan answered, “The Lord also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die. Howbeit, because by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the child also that is born unto thee shall surely die.”

That is both halves of Exodus 34:7. David got pardoned, but he did not get cleared. The punishment was still coming: one part the men of Israel dying in battle, the other his son having to die and his house having nothing but trouble. The judgment of David was that child being put to death.

precepts.text: Godly sorrow worketh repentance unto salvation, but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
precepts.point: Through David's judgment, Solomon was still able to be born; it was all part of the plan of the Most High. The backup master plan behind everything was Christ, who still had to be born through David's lineage; David was still loved and still forgiven, which shows repentance, and that even the mighty among us can fall and yet rise back up.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

precepts.why:
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.”

David’s sorrow was godly sorrow, and it worked repentance. Through the judgment, “David comforted Bath–sheba his wife”, and she bare a son, “and he called his name Solomon: and the Lord loved him.” The Lord sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, who called his name Jedidiah, “because of the Lord.”

David was still loved and still forgiven, and that shows repentance. Through David’s judgment Solomon was still able to be born; it was all part of the plan of the Most High. The backup master plan behind everything was Christ, who still had to be born through David’s lineage.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

precepts.why:
“My flesh trembleth for fear of thee; and I am afraid of thy judgments.”

David had felt the judgment of the Most High. He was pardoned, but the child that was born to him surely died, as Nathan said. His repentance was not a light thing; it came from a man afraid of the Lord’s judgments. Out of that repentance Solomon was born, and the Lord loved him.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

precepts.why:
“For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.”

David fell, and he rose up again. He was judged, he repented, and the Lord still loved him and gave him Solomon, whom Nathan called Jedidiah because of the Lord. Even the mighty among us can fall and yet rise back up.

precepts.text: The Most High would raise up evil out of David's own house and give his wives to his neighbour in the sight of the sun, done before all Israel because David did it secretly.
precepts.point: Ahithophel counselled Absalom to lie with the ten concubines David left, in the sight of all Israel, on the roof of the house. This is the exact fulfillment of what the Most High spoke in chapter 12, that David's wives would be taken and one would lie with them in the sight of the sun, and that what David did secretly would be done before all Israel. It was not coincidence or irony; it was prophesied to happen, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did. The Most High keeps mercy and forgives, but by no means clears the guilty, so even when we come in and repent, we still must remember the fear of the Most High, for there is but one step between us and death.

note.label: 2 Samuel 16: Ziba, Shimei's Cursing, and Absalom Defiles the Concubines

precepts.why:
The Most High told David by Nathan, “Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes, and give them unto thy neighbour, and he shall lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun. For thou didst it secretly: but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.”

Here it is. Ahithophel counselled Absalom, “Go in unto thy father’s concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father”. So “they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.” The ten concubines David left, on the roof of the house, in the sight of the sun.

This is the exact fulfillment of what the Most High spoke in chapter 12. It was not coincidence or irony; it was prophesied to happen. What David did secretly was done before all Israel, by evil raised up out of his own house, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did.

moments.label: Blasphemers & Traitors: Judge Not Before the Time

points: The Lord sent Nathan unto David with the parable of the rich man who spared his own flock and took the poor man's one little ewe lamb. David's anger was greatly kindled: the man that hath done this thing shall surely die. And Nathan said, thou art the man. The rich man is you, David; the poor man was Uriah the Hittite, and the ewe lamb was his wife.

note.label: Blasphemers & Traitors: Judge Not Before the Time

points: Nathan had to approach David with a parable, because at this point David was out of his right mind; approach him the wrong way and he could have been killed too. Once the example gave David conviction, he came to his senses: I have sinned against the Lord.

The Lord said, what thou didst secretly, I will do this thing before all Israel: the sword shall never depart from thine house. And Nathan said, the Lord also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die. But evil stayed in David's house perpetually: the trouble among his sons, his own counsellor turning against him, being chased out of his kingdom. David was never the same after this.

note.label: Blasphemers & Traitors: Judge Not Before the Time

points: Howbeit, because by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the child also that is born unto thee shall surely die. It would get around that the king God chose killed a man for his wife. Your actions gave the enemies occasion to speak evil of the Lord: to insult him through what you did.

note.label: Blasphemers & Traitors: Judge Not Before the Time

points: Nathan came to David with a parable. When David judged that the man deserved to die for taking the poor man's one lamb, he was unknowingly pronouncing sentence on himself.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

points: The Most High sent Nathan unto David, who told him of two men in one city, one rich and one poor. The rich man had many flocks and herds, but the poor man had nothing save one little ewe lamb he had bought and nourished up, which was unto him as a daughter. When a traveler came, the rich man spared his own flock and took the poor man's lamb. David's anger was greatly kindled, and he said the man that had done this shall surely die and restore the lamb fourfold, because he had no pity.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

points: Nathan said unto David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the Most High: I anointed thee king over Israel, delivered thee out of the hand of Saul, gave thee thy master's house and wives, and the house of Israel and of Judah, and would have given thee more. Wherefore hast thou despised the commandment to do evil, killing Uriah the Hittite with the sword and taking his wife, slaying him with the sword of the children of Ammon?

The Most High said if David would have just asked, He would have given him anything, for He had already given him the kingdom, Saul's house, and protection from Saul. The commandment David despised was what was read in Deuteronomy 27. There is a term called suicide by cop; David committed murder by the hand of another nation, because he set the whole thing up.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

points: Thus saith the Most High: Now therefore the sword shall never depart from thine house, because thou hast despised me and taken the wife of Uriah to be thy wife. Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes and give them unto thy neighbour, who shall lie with them in the sight of the sun. Thou didst it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.
As the four chapters go on, and beyond, you are going to see the fruition of what just happened worked out in David's own house.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

points: The judgment of David was that child being put to death. This goes back to Exodus 34: the Most High keeps mercy and forgives iniquity, but will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children. David got pardoned, but he did not get cleared; the punishment was still coming, one part the men of Israel dying in battle, the other his son having to die and his house having nothing but trouble.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

points: David said unto Nathan, I have sinned against the Most High. Nathan said the Most High hath also put away thy sin; thou shalt not die. Howbeit, because by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the Most High to blaspheme, the child also that is born unto thee shall surely die.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

points: Nathan departed, and the Most High struck the child, so that it was very sick. David besought God for the child, fasted, and lay all night upon the earth, refusing to rise or eat with the elders of his house. On the seventh day the child died, and the servants feared to tell him. When David perceived by their whispering that the child was dead, he arose, washed, anointed himself, changed his apparel, worshiped in the house of the Most High, and then ate bread. When asked why, he said that while the child lived he fasted and wept, for who could tell whether God would be gracious; but now the child was dead, he could not bring him back, he would go to him but the child would not return to him.

David did all the fasting and prayer before the child died because he knew it was of the Most High that this would happen; no amount of prayer would bring the child back. David was content, saying he did not want it to happen but had no choice in the matter, for the Most High had said it would be so.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

points: David comforted Bathsheba his wife, went in unto her, and she bare a son, and he called his name Solomon; and the Most High loved him, and sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, who called his name Jedidiah, because of the Most High.

Through David's judgment, Solomon was still able to be born; it was all part of the plan of the Most High. The backup master plan behind everything was Christ, who still had to be born through David's lineage; David was still loved and still forgiven, which shows repentance, and that even the mighty among us can fall and yet rise back up.

note.label: 2 Samuel 12: Nathan's Parable and the Judgment on David's House

points: Joab fought against Rabbah of the children of Ammon and took the royal city, then sent for David to gather the rest of the people and take the city, lest it be called after Joab's name. David gathered all the people, went to Rabbah, took it, and took the king's crown of a talent of gold with the precious stones, and set it on his head. He brought forth great spoil, put the people to labor under saws and axes of iron and to the brickkiln, and did so unto all the cities of Ammon, then returned to Jerusalem.

David won against the children of Ammon once again. What we gather from these four chapters is that David was called, he was king, a very mighty man, but he slipped and fell; he had godly sorrow, and in that godly sorrow he was not put to death. If he had been, there would be no Solomon, and through that no Christ. The only one perfect in this world was Christ, in whom there was no iniquity; but the men before us, when they failed, had godly sorrow, repented, and kept the commandments of the Most High even after they fell, rising back up again.
